research_questions.q: Why is my Mysore masala dosa not crispy?
source_answers: Batter should be flowy, not watery and not thick — watery sticks, thick stays soft.
Use a well-heated iron tawa; sprinkle water to test sizzle before spreading.
Oil around the edges helps crispness; too much oil makes it greasy and less crisp.
Restaurant-style Mysore dosa is crisp outside and a little soft/spongy inside — not a paper roast.

research_questions.q: Why does my dosa stick to the pan?
source_answers: Pan neither too hot nor too cold — water should sizzle, not explode into steam.
Batter should be creamy; too thick or poorly ground batter sticks.
Iron tawa needs seasoning with oil (onion-oil rub is a common home fix). Non-stick does not need onion rub.
If the tawa is too hot, batter lumps and will not spread thin.

research_questions.q: What makes Mysore masala dosa different from regular masala dosa?
source_answers: The difference is the fiery red chilli-garlic chutney smeared inside before the potato filling.
Authentic Mysore style is crisp outside with a slightly spongy bite inside, often golden-brown.
Regular masala dosa is the crepe plus potato palya; Mysore adds that red chutney layer.

research_questions.q: Should dosa batter be thick or thin?
source_answers: For crisp dosa, batter should pour like thin cream / thin pancake batter — spreadable, not stiff.
Too thick traps moisture and cooks like a pancake. Too thin tears and will not crisp.
After fermentation, add water a little at a time until it spreads in one circular motion.

research_questions.q: Why does the potato filling make my dosa soggy?
source_answers: Add potato masala only at the end, once the dosa has set.
Filling should be moist, not watery — wet palya soaks the crepe.
Eat immediately; sitting after folding loses crispness.
